explanation: No consistent token or context. Top hits mix Apache .htaccess/Rewrite config lines, XML config indentation, code punctuation, and ordinary prose tokens such as commas in place names, 'the', 'a', 'and'. Mid and weak hits are scattered function words.

Fires mostly on content nouns in scientific or medical abstract prose, especially 'safety' (as in 'assess the safety of'), 'mechanism(s)', 'number' ('a number of'), 'horizontal', 'oxygen' and 'superoxide'. The top hit, an SVG path command letter, is an outlier. Generic prose and function words give weak or no activation.

Fires strongly on the opening parenthesis that follows a spelled-out multi-word technical name and comes right before its acronym, e.g. 'ATP-binding cassette (ABC)' or 'Total knee arthroplasty (TKA)'. Weaker offshoots: the colon in 'Nasdaq: TICKER' or a subtitle, and the first digit of a yardage or year number. The top-of-range acronym '(' is the clear main job.

Fires on function words and number tokens inside biographical or encyclopedic phrasing about a person's achievements and timeline, e.g. 'graduated in/as', 'diploma from', 'win of the year', 'the 2013 [prize]', 'nine-time', 'former member'. The second digit of an award or event year is a typical hit. Outside biography-like text it is weak.

Mostly fires on tokens in non-English or rare-word contexts: sentence-final punctuation and newlines in Russian forum questions, word pieces inside rare proper names and Latin taxonomic or technical words (e.g. 'tym' in 'tympani', 'Lozouet', 'Méndez'), German and Indonesian text. It looks like a generic unfamiliar-text or tokenization feature, without one sharp trigger.

Its clearest job is the first digit of the day number in a date written month-first or day-first ('May [2]3', 'July [1]1', '[1]5 August'). It also fires on early function words in short question or intro sentences ('What does [it] mean', 'Here's [a]', 'First [of] all') and on some code tokens. The date-day digit is the dominant pattern.

Fires on nouns and word pieces for things worn or wrapped around a body or object (belt, collar, band, cap, bikini, corset, scarf, bracelets, watchband, armor), and on ring- or ridge-shaped structures (rings, annulus/annular, escarpment). Activation is on the noun token or its final subword. Unrelated words are weak.

Fires on Go source-code tokens, especially 'package' at the start of a Go file after the license header, '.com' in 'github.com/...' import paths, 'Code generated by go-swagger', and Go syntax ('func (', '*Command', 'import ('). Weaker on similar boilerplate in Python setup and docstrings. A few line breaks in poetry and German text are outliers.

Fires on subword pieces inside non-English words (German, Norwegian/Danish, Hungarian, Turkish, Somali, Hindi) and inside personal names in copyright-header email addresses ('Fl[orian].Rival@', 're[ne]@gollent'). The hit is a mid-word continuation token in a non-English or name string. English prose gives little activation.

Fires most strongly on 'subject' in the PHP license boilerplate 'This source file is subject to the ... License' (Zend, Magento). Below that it fires moderately on a broad, unrelated mix: other license text, math word pieces (irreducible, Cauchy-Schwarz), code tokens and prose. Only the top pattern is sharp.

Fires on tokens in cryptocurrency and cryptography text: Bitcoin/SegWit, mining, public/private keys, signing or generating certificates, Monero, E-Gold, proof-of-work, sha256. A secondary cluster is endocrine and pharmacology terms (gonadotropin, somatotropin, orexigenic, GLP-1 'long acting').

Hits are diverse. Recurring ones: 'the' after 'won'/'win'/'received' before a prize or championship name, the space before a year or event number in sports listings, and pieces of person names. Others are Objective-C/Swift code tokens ('canImport', 'WithIndex', 'Exception') and scattered medical words. No single shared trigger.

Fires on plural or result nouns in scientific methods/results prose (tissues, isolates, xenografts, transformants, patients, experiments, figures, values), on comparison tokens between numbers ('77 versus 64', '+/-'), and on '/blob' in GitHub URLs. Also on some reporting verbs and prepositions in news prose ('spoke to', 'quoted').

Fires inside opaque identifier or code strings: hex digits in colors and UUIDs (the '-' separators in UUIDs), postcode digits, Objective-C class-name prefixes ('ABC', 'LM'), struct names, and chemistry word pieces like 'carbonyl'. It responds to characters in the middle of non-word alphanumeric strings, not to the identity of a particular token.
